title: The Substance has a lot going for it, but the story makes it nonsensical for no reason

commenti.body:
at first, there is just one shared consciousness transferred between the bodies.

the experience is akin to being an addict getting high. you're either high or you're low—now, because of how society reinforces the distinctions between how the two bodies experience life, her personality does begin to split, until they become utterly divided. but it didn't start that way.

Remember their one and the same lol. You gotta really suspend disbelief watching this movie. At the end of the day it’s just a genre film I don’t think it’s pretending to be higher art or anything. It’s nonsensical plot kinda adds to its whole vibe for me. It’s all style no substance.

i think this is a cogent criticism of how the film sort of loses its thread in the back half of the film. i don't feel like the writer/director had a full handle on the character and thematic development beyond the initial concept and the first week or two of the character living separate lives. beyond that, it just doesn't really hold up or sustain my interest, because i guess the point of the film is that the character is inescapably vain and will now be punished for her mistakes.

I think Elisabeth wants to believe she is Sue, because the alternative is worst. When she doesn’t go on that date, you can see why she’s not very motivated to continue existing as herself. 
She eventually gets to the point where her body is so degraded, she can’t even bring herself to terminate the experience. But I think we see she had already started spiraling way before the experience even started. It’s sad!

I think there's a theme of living vicariously through your child. Elizabeth 'births' Sue who goes on to experience a life she can't live and even though she's extremely envious, it's all she has. It's sad. At least, that's what I got from it. Maybe it can be a metaphor addiction too. The substance is a drug, Elizabeth is the addict destroying herself and Sue is symbol for getting high. Just an idea. 

In literal terms though, I agree that Elizabeth not actually experiencing the life Sue is living is confusing since the movie repeats "you are one" over and over again. They don't share consciousness. Sue is dependent on Elizabeth to live. Elizabeth has the option to "terminate" (which goes along with the motherhood theme that I personally gravitate to). 

I think the movie aims to be seen more allegorical than literal so I'm not super hung up on the plot of characters. The movie is better when you try to think about what they represent. I would argue that wondering "why would she do this" is exactly the point of the movie.

Personally, I interpreted it less as if they were really two separated experiential wholes and more that Elizabeth's sense of self was so rooted in how she was perceived by others that she couldn't stand ever being Elizabeth once she got to be Sue.

I had the same thought, and I think the movie recognizes the same issue and does comment on it. There is a moment in the film where Elisabeth basically flat out says it, that Sue is the only part of her that's worth anything, that matters. Even if it's not her directly, it's a version of her that other people value. Her only self-worth comes from the validation of other people. So, by people valuing Sue, she feels that they value her even if she doesn't get to experience it firsthand.

There is a specific parallels in real life that I'll suggest can help explain how she might feel towards Sue. Bad parents often use their children as a proxy for themselves. Simone de Beauvoir made this specific point in The Second Sex. Some women who have daughters use them as a way to relive their youth. They'll enter them into pageants, dress them up, force them into hobbies that they failed to take up, etc. You see this all the time in beauty pageants where the mom is the one who is really into it and the daughter just looks exploited. For sons, they use them as a way to experience the privilege of a patriarchal society that they'd otherwise be excluded from (this one's way more complicated to get into so I'll leave it alone). The point being, these parents do not actually experience the lives of their children in any way. They are outsiders observing on the sidelines. Like Elisabeth is for Sue. Yet, they still derive a significant pleasure/satisfaction from vicariously living the life of another whom they have a sense of possession over. It's like, if that's my child, then their accomplishments/value are also mine. So, that would be how I rationalize how Elisabeth feels towards Sue. She sees Sue in the same way that a bad parent sees their child. As a means to live out vicariously their failures/dreams.
[removed]
Pun intended?

>At the end of the day it’s just a genre film I don’t think it’s pretending to be higher art or anything.

Cannes really fell off

Okay, but…she does remember and consciously experience herself as Sue? Your whole summary of how the movie would be better if they had the same conscious experience is…literally the way the move is?

I get why it doesn’t seem that way, cause they both seem so indignant and surprised at the others’ behavior the day after they wake up as the other, but this is not because they literally don’t remember, it’s because the whole switch is a metaphor for body dysmorphia and dissociation. 

When you have severe body dysmorphia you literally don’t see your self the way others see you—you don’t identify with your body. Dissociation works the same way, where you feel as if you’re almost just watching your body do things from the outside, sometimes things that you don’t imagine yourself as ever doing. You become so detached and out of touch with your self, often in combination with an acute self-hate, that you don’t feel like you have any control at all over yourself. 

This movie takes that very real mental phenomenon and turns it into a physical phenomenon—imagine someone suffering from body dysmorphia and dissociation then literally separated the two versions of themselves into two people embodying those two extremes physically. It wouldn’t take very much at all to completely dissociate to the point of feeling like you have absolutely no control or accountability over the other. That’s why the customer service rep over the phone keeps telling her that they are the same, because they are—she just cannot accept that, because each side of her hates the other so totally.

Yup. And it's extremely blatant in its presentation. If you watched this movie and don't believe that they are the same person with overlapping experiences, you watched it wrong. Plain and simple.

The movie literally gives you a talking head flashback to help you remember an interaction from less than an hour prior. Twice. It's not presenting information for you to ignore. "They are one" is so simple, and essential for understanding the weight of the conflict towards the end.

I think the movie could have played out the way it was if at the start it was set up as her experiencing being Sue, and the bigger split happening later the more it gets worse to be Elizabeth in comparison. 

But the way it was set up, the motivation to continue makes no sense.

Just the fact it needed to be repeated so many times kind of makes the point. Why not really make it Elizabeth's experience at first, and it would be psychologically justifiable to explain why she'd fuck up the balance and even eventually "split" mentally

I agree with this comment, and think it also applies to the film’s supposed feminist message. It starts off as a valid critique of the horrifying treatment of older women in Hollywood, but by the end, it condones the humiliation of women for attempting to conform to unrealistic beauty standards. The audience is meant to laugh at Sparkle’s final form, just as we laugh at women with uncanny plastic surgery.

I was under the impression that Elisabeth remembers everything she does as Sue. *italic text* That *italic text* is exactly what makes her time as Elisabeth so unbearable: the contrast. 

As Elisabeth she’s over-the-hill by the shallow industry standards she can’t get away from. As Sue she dominates that industry and is everything everyone wants her to be. 

If it were a Severence type situation where she remembered nothing as Sue, the contrast wouldn’t hurt. It’s fine to be your normal self if that’s all you know. But once you’ve tasted something sweeter, that normal self starts to become unbearable, which is what the old guy/young medical worker who followed her to the diner tells her.

Yeah but to get to the point of her body being that degraded, she had to keep bringing back sue. But if she isn't feeling Sue, why the fuck would she do it? Not even the moment after her finger got fucked, i mean even after the very first take. If it's not you, what's the use? 


But if it was her conscious mind inside, it would actually make sense. And it would all still work, it would just be her conscious self being too high on the experience and not wanting to go back, then fucking up, making the normal life worse etc

Maybe. Maybe also I fundamentally never understood parents so the whole logic makes no sense to me 


But I think all the allegory would make perfect, in fact even more sense, if it was Elisabeth. Then it would be the drug effect, the addiction would make sense.

I think that plot point is fine. Imagine there were two versions of you: same brain, but different bodies and no shared memories. It’s kind of deterministic, but the idea is that you would do completely different things when you have different bodies and then the completely same thing when you have the same body. Body A knows that she can’t judge Body B because everything Body B does is exactly what she would do if she had that body. It makes complete sense.

What I mainly find nonsensical however is that a big star would walk into some shady corner to pick up a cosmetic drug suggested to her by some random nurse, in a world where it is not implied that the suggested effect of the drug is possible in any way.

This is just one stupid thing among other stupid things in a largely stupid film that I didn’t really enjoy. I can’t believe it won a screenplay award lol. The world of the film (I accept that it doesn’t take place in our world) is just poorly designed.

Yeah. My read on it was that Elizabeth's sense of self was so wrapped up in her appearance and how she was perceived by others that she doesn't have anything to live for when she isn't Sue, especially when she starts to be "deformed" by staying as Sue for too long. It's not that they were distinct consciousness as much as there was one life she felt was worth living and one that wasn't

> There is a moment in the film where Elisabeth basically flat out says it, that Sue is the only part of her that's worth anything, that matters.

Yeah but that fell flat for me because Sue was never being Elisabeth. If it was her, then it would make sense and I think all elements would work really well 


Someone else mentioned the parental parallel here, maybe I don't get it. I never really understood what makes people create something else to add anything to their lives. It's just another rando.

I think Sue is all she has. The adoration that Sue gets, knowing that it’s a piece of her that people are adoring, that’s enough for Elisabeth. I think right before she is about to terminate, she starts thinking about how everyone will admire her at the New Years Eve event and realizes she wants that more than her body back.

I think it tries to drive this theme at the end when you see ElisaSue as one single being. We see Demi Moore’s face reappear in the new body so we know she’s one and the same now, and she performs for the audience. For us!! It was more important to have the show go on than for Elisabeth to go back to her body and continue living & hating herself.

I am quite confused by your and the others' criticism of the plot, as the film clearly shows that she remember part of the experience (such as the motorcyclist), yet does not remember other parts. The film definitely never outright states what the memory of each person looks like.

I thought that it being ambiguous on that matter was a good move on part of the filmmakers as it makes the experience of watching the film similarly desorienting as it must be for a person taking the drug.

Yeah the two separate experiences and lack of memory does obscure the point of the movie, but I think that's a strength.

For example, I was wondering why Elizabeth doesn't just write a letter to Sue. Like, I feel there's a scenario where they just communicate with each other and share their 7 days productively. Then it occurs to me that the movie could also represent a toxic relationship. So again, it's not an airtight plot but the more I sit with it is a really interesting movie from many different perspectives.

This is basically how I took it. 

To me, it seemed like they the conscious experience of being the “other person” feels something like a dream when the switch over happens, so the memories are hazier and disorienting.

But how is Sue anything Elisabeth has if she isn't experiencing it? 

I understand that in theory "they are one" but it is clearly not something overtly experienced. So what's the point?

I think they do share consciousness (at least until she fails to terminate), but she compartmentalizes because she doesn't want to take responsibility. She turned to The Substance in a moment of weakness, so of course she doesn't take seriously the sort of diligence needed to use it properly, and the ever-increasing divide between young "Sue" and beat-up old Elizabeth takes a major psychological toll which really messes up her perspective.
In my mind, Sue was created from a piece of Elisabeth so that’s why she sees people’s adoration of Sue as an adoration of Elisabeth.

>but by the end, it condones the humiliation of women for attempting to conform to unrealistic beauty standards. The audience is meant to laugh at Sparkle’s final form, just as we laugh at women with uncanny plastic surgery. 

I don't agree with that reading at all, honestly. There *are* darkly funny moments in that end sequence, but I feel like you're meant to at the very least feel challenged by, or reflect on why you laughed. The complete lack of any sympathetic portrayal of the likes of Harvey in the audience, Elisasue's pleading and telling the audience 'I'm still the same person', and the parallels in presentation between that scene and Joseph Merrick in the Elephant Man, all combined to make me believe that Fargeat didn't intended for her to be anything but a tragic figure in those moments.
They are the same consciousness

If I had no memories, my "other me" wouldn't matter to me. I either experience it, or it's just irrelevant. Someone else. 


I agree that overall screenplay is surreal but I can accept that much as a setup

If you met a random stranger that looked exactly like you, I think you would treat that person much differently than you would treat any other person. Either much nicer or much meaner than normal, depending on how you think of yourself. That’s how I look at it…

She doesn't remember though. Both of them are shown surprised and unaware of what they did. Elisabeth needs to see the interview with Sue to know what got said. 


If they just made them share the experience everything would fit in well

The movie could have shown this through some gradual progression, instead it treats them as two different entities who know nothing about what the other is doing, aside from literally saying they're one, because even the characters don't get it. That's not strong enough to explain why Elisabeth would give Sue her time of day she takes no conscious part in. 


The whole idea would have worked perfectly if it was just her though.

What's the point of taking a drug when you don't remember the experience? 

She didn't remember the cyclist, she had a horror dream about him. Much different than an experience that leaves you wanting more
But why should she give any fucks about sue if she isn't experiencing sue as if it's her?
It doesn't justify why Elisabeth would ever go back to being sue after not being fully conscious the first time. If it's not her, what's the point?
But it's not her so what's the kick?
But she's not experiencing it as herself. When she's Elisabeth she doesn't remember it as a great experience. She just doesn't remember it. Which makes it pointless
I get your point

Of course the characters don’t get it, they’re the ones suffering from it.

I don’t even understand what you mean by “some gradual progression,” the progression of her dissociation IS gradual. 

“It” doesn’t treat them as two different entities who know nothing about what the other is doing, “it” constantly tells them and the viewer that they are the same. 

That literally explains why Elisabeth would give Sue her time of day, because she DOES take a conscious part in it., because she knows somewhere in her that they are the same, she just can’t accept the bad with the good. The idea works exactly as intended, because she IS just her.
I watched that movie under the impression that she *was* fully conscious and just lying to herself to avoid responsibility.
That doesn't add up to what we saw. It could have been effectively demonstrated as a process of separation.

She does remember it as a great experience, otherwise she wouldn’t continue to do it. We see this happen in real-time at the end when she second-guesses herself about terminating the Sue body—she literally switches in a matter of seconds between seeing Sue as a foreign enemy to seeing her as a part of herself (the only “good” part of herself, at that).
If she doesn't remember what experience she had that week, there's no reason for her to have it again.

We don't see it at all throughout the movie, this had to be established at the start. We see her falling to it at the end where she's a deformed freak. It doesn't even come from any memory retention as much as it comes from why the fuck is she still living like that. 

It would all make much more sense if she very literally had both experiences

You never see her happy about the experience do you? That would make a difference in how we view Elizabeth. Instead, we see her bored at home passing time until the next experience. That's where I see the drug addiction metaphor, but I agree she doesn't have much motivation when taken literally and I think it's a valid critique.

You’re right, there wouldn’t be any reason if she doesn’t remember. Which is why it makes more sense to assume she does. 

>>For all intents and purposes, it’s a different person.

This I don’t entirely disagree with, because yes that is what it feels like when you’re dissociating to that degree. But the fact of the matter is that she *does* remember, and they *are* the same. She is told that from the beginning, and that is the truth of the matter.

But they very clearly and consistently don't remember each other's experiences aside from on some subconscious, vague dream level. Thats why we all (including the characters) need to be consistently told they're one. 

Which is stupid in terms of storytelling as the story would be much better if they did remember and actually were one consciousness to start with

Elisabeth didn’t need to watch it to see what was said. Watching the interview served to reenforce how eager people are to embrace Sue and forget Elisabeth. Sue isn’t going to speak too kindly of Elisabeth because she’s more eager to forget her than anyone else. 

I don’t think there are any cases of one being genuinely unaware of the actions of the other.

Why do you think they don’t remember each other’s experience? There’s nothing in the film that proves that concretely, they simply act surprised at the evidence of the other’s behavior, but again this can be explained just as easily and more accurately to the themes of the film as a consequence of dissociation.

And the film specifically emphasizes the split over time to portray the growing extremity of the dissociation, by gradually refusing to portray to the audience the full events of each persona, and instead chooses to portray them from the perspective of the opposite persona to make it feel more like they are a different person, to try and instill the feeling that the character feels in the audience. But it does not indicate that they are different consciousnesses or that they don’t remember, only that they are self-hating and self-deceiving. 

How about this: if Elisabeth literally didn’t remember her actions in Sue’s body, why wouldn’t she argue with the guy on the phone? If you literally couldn’t control your other self, but the guy kept telling you you can, wouldn’t you argue with him? Wouldn’t you threaten to sue (ha) them, or at least assume something is wrong with the substance, since they’re telling you it should work one way but you’re experiencing it another? But Elisabeth doesn’t do this, she doesn’t even argue at all with the representative, because deep down she knows that she is ultimately in control. She knows it’s all up to her, but she can’t give it up.

What you call “stupid in terms of storytelling,” I call a clever and obviously purposeful rhetorical technique to get the viewer to empathize with what it feels like to suffer from body dysmorphia and dissociative tendencies.

She doesn’t care about herself, she just wants to feel the adoration of the audience - even if it’s indirect! 

That’s my takeaway at least. I’m reading a bit of the rest of the thread and I totally get your read too. I can conceptually understand the pride that a parent has for their child (as an extension of themselves) but it’s not something I can really comprehend logically in my head cuz I’ve never experienced it lol.

>What's the point of taking a drug when you don't remember the experience? 

I am not quite sure why you are asking me this, because I am arguing that they indeed remember some of the experience.

>She didn't remember the cyclist, she had a horror dream about him.

Yes, the memory was not accurate but there are parts of that vision that are memories: that she brought the cyclist home, the face of the cyclist, that they did have sex. The film is vague about how much of the memizy they actually share. It could very well be that they remember most of the experience, even if it certainly not all.

We're told over and over again that they are one, curious why so many folks don't want to believe that. The way Elisabeth and Sue act like they are not one, is a physical representation of how they try to avoid personal accountability and responsibility. A representation of how our experiences in one body and mind can be so disjointed. Like you have a new years resolution to eat healthy and then the next day can't stop yourself from eating fried chicken for dinner. Or you're trying to become sober and end up blackout drunk one day. It's a great metaphor (a very obvious one I'd say) for how we fail to accept different parts of ourselves. Also a metaphor for stealing from the future version of ourselves by actively doing things to harm ourself in pursuit of pleasure. I think The Substance is full of these types of physical embodiments of psychological phenomena. Like when after Elisabeth eats a lot of fried chicken, it literally goes to Sue's butt, like how we say oh no I can't eat this it'll go straight to my butt or chin or wherever. It's brilliant!

>  I think The Substance is full of these types of physical embodiments of psychological phenomena. Like when after Elisabeth eats a lot of fried chicken, it literally goes to Sue's butt, like how we say oh no I can't eat this it'll go straight to my butt or chin or wherever

I wouldn't call that brilliant, those scenes were too on the nose. But I didn't mind either cause obviously it wanted to be like that. The execution still made it clumsy


The repetition of the fact that they're one exactly shows that they wouldn't know otherwise. Yeah, probably everyone experienced some version of getting lost in a moment and doing something, then later when you feel the consequences of it, wishing you didn't or almost not even understanding why you did anymore or even feeling like you acted like a different person (e.g. being drunk is a common example) 


Which is why it's a failure not to show that the experience is shared, since the split would work. From the very first try, Elisabeth shows no signs of having experienced anything Sue did. There's no initial excitement, or looking forward to the next trip from her side. The way they remember things is at best a blurry dream, with many instances that show they don't even remember at all 

You can wish you didn't get that drunk, you can even feel like you don't even want to drink again when you wake up hungover, you can even forget a lot of it or not understand why you did something. But at least you still remember how it started, how it felt to start. When you feel like getting drunk again, you look forward to it. 

I can see how eventually the whole thing can progress into a compulsion that doesn't even feel good and that she disassociated from, but at the beginning the connection needed to be there to show that the experience was a great trip for her. But in the movie she disconnected from the start which made no sense. We never saw her getting anything from the experience. 


Now I think it took the metaphor too literally in that too on the nose sense (avoiding responsibility), and is another movie that sacrificed the logic of the story for it. It wasn't necessary

Interesting discussion! FWIW, I had the same impression as OP. At the beginning of the movie I thought the two bodies would share one memory, but from the first transformation the movie seemed to make a point of showing there is no retention of memory between the 2 characters (except some vague dream imagery). At least I don't recall either of them explicitly remembering any event the other character did. It's a bit surprising to me so many people here have the opposite impression though.

I like the point that Elisabeth might just be living vicariously through Sue, although in that reading I find it strange that she would keep Sue's body locked away during her 7 days (while it is perfectly logical why Sue would rather forget about Elisabeth's body). I'd expect her to fawn over the younger body (perhaps even fall in love with it?) while she's waiting until she can switch again.

No, when Sue extended her time for the first time Elisabeth was completely unaware. She said so in her phone call with the Substance company. They are not sharing a consciousness or communicating.

Obviously, in their individual selves they see what the other has built or destroyed, but when Elisabeth is unconscious she is *not* experiencing Sue.

I think maybe for Elisabeth the idea of it is enough.
For better or worse Sue's triumphs are hers. Even in abstraction. Because Sue is made of her. 

I have a mother who lived vicariously through me and who claimed all my successes. 

I do think, the film is actually quite overt in that, it's about motherhood. Or a specific narcissistic type of it anyway.
I don't get how they're hers in any way if she's not experiencing it

I think this has become abundantly clear throughout this thread. Haha. Probably a good thing. :)

There is a subsection of people that just become really psychologically enmeshed with others.
At least at the beginning they could show how great she felt and how that made the time as Elisabeth worse, like how being sober can be hard
